name: Kaya identity
seoDesc: Kaya identity: work out energy intensity of the GDP from the population and the GDP per capita. A free ecology calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Supply the population, the GDP per capita, the energy carbon footprint and the impact and the Kaya identity calculator solves for energy intensity of the GDP. It is built for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Kaya identity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Kaya identity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports energy intensity of the GDP in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the population, the GDP per capita, the energy carbon footprint and the impact (CO₂ emissions).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Kaya identity calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Energy intensity of the GDP=impact (CO₂ emissions) ÷ (GDP per capita × energy carbon footprint × population)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Kaya identity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the population, the GDP per capita and the energy carbon footprint — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Kaya identity calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — population for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Kaya identity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns energy intensity of the GDP, derived from the population, the GDP per capita and the energy carbon footprint. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Kaya identity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the population, the GDP per capita, the energy carbon footprint and the impact, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Impact (CO₂ emissions) = 161393474742.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Kaya identity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
